topic: Unsloth v0.1.801-beta lets you reach Unsloth Desktop from another device on your own network
title: Unsloth LAN access without Cloudflare
description:
Unsloth LAN access: reach your local model from another device on your own network, no Cloudflare tunnel.

Unsloth binds to itself by default, which is why the box in the other room ignores your laptop. One setting or one flag changes that, and Unsloth stops and forces you to replace the admin password it generated before the switch will move. The part the release notes do not lead with: server-side tools run as your user, so anyone reaching that server with your API key can run code on that machine.

You'll learn: why the default bind is 127.0.0.1, the two ways to open it to your network, why the password change is not optional, and when to pass --disable-tools.

Sources are in the pinned comment. (narration is ai-generated using the creator's own cloned voice)

#Unsloth #LocalAI #LANAccess

narration_full: Your model runs on the box in the other room. You are on the couch, and Unsloth will not answer your laptop. That is not a bug. By default Unsloth answers on one twenty-seven dot zero dot zero dot one. That address is loopback. It is the one a machine uses to talk to itself. So nothing outside that machine can reach it. That is deliberate. Unsloth does document a Cloudflare tunnel, a relay that gives your server a public web address. That tunnel is the right tool from a hotel. From your own couch, it routes your rig through somebody else's service. To reach a room away. Step one: open Settings and switch on network access. Or launch it with the host flag set to all zeros. Either one is a wildcard bind. Unsloth listens on every address the machine has, not just its own. Step two: change the admin password Unsloth generated for you. It stops and asks, because the toggle will not move until you do. Now pick up the laptop. Unsloth shows you the address to type and a code you can scan. The toggle takes effect without a restart, so nothing has to reload. Here is the part the release notes do not lead with. Server-side tools run as your user. Anyone who reaches that server with your API key can run code on that machine. That is Unsloth's own banner. It sits on the same docs page as the tunnel. Network reach and code execution are the same switch here. So pass the disable tools flag unless you meant to hand that out. Now Unsloth answers your laptop from the other room, with nothing in the path. The password change is forced, and the tools decision is yours.

scenes.visual_brief: Frame 1: a phosphor terminal window already fills the frame, its prompt line reading UNSLOTH WON'T ANSWER FROM THE COUCH in pale green, a small couch glyph parked lower left. Motion onset at 0.3s: the block cursor pops on and blinks beside the last character. At 2s a second machine glyph fades in at the far right and a wall is drawn between the two. At 5s a request packet slides from the couch toward the wall, stops dead against it, and the prompt returns a red refused line.

At 4s a thin box draws itself around the machine glyph and the address slides inside it. At 7s the label THIS MACHINE ONLY fades up beneath, and every arrow pointing in from outside the box dims to muted grey.

scenes.narration: So nothing outside that machine can reach it. That is deliberate. Unsloth does document a Cloudflare tunnel, a relay that gives your server a public web address.
scenes.visual_brief: Hard cut to two labelled columns. At 1s the left column draws the couch, the wall and the dead request from the hook. At 4s the right column types a Cloudflare route: your box, out to the internet, back to your phone. At 7s the words PUBLIC WEB ADDRESS land under the right column in amber and a small globe pops beside them.

scenes.on_screen_text: your couch is not a hotel
scenes.visual_brief: The Cloudflare route stretches across the full frame as one long looping line. At 2s a hotel glyph appears at the far end and the loop lights green, reading as correct. At 5s the hotel swaps for the couch glyph two metres from the box, and the same long loop stays lit. At 8s the loop pulses once and a muted label draws beneath it: ONE ROOM AWAY.

scenes.narration: Step one: open Settings and switch on network access. Or launch it with the host flag set to all zeros. Either one is a wildcard bind. Unsloth listens on every address the machine has, not just its own.
scenes.visual_brief: Hard cut to a Settings panel drawn as a terminal menu. At 2s the LAN access row highlights and its toggle switches from off to on with a stepped snap. At 5s the panel slides left and a command line types unsloth studio -H 0.0.0.0 beneath it. At 8s the run of zeros pulses amber. At 10s the machine glyph sprouts an arrow on every side, one per address it now answers on.

scenes.narration: Step two: change the admin password Unsloth generated for you. It stops and asks, because the toggle will not move until you do.
scenes.on_screen_text: LAN access off until password changed
scenes.visual_brief: Hard cut to a password prompt, the generated string shown as a row of masked blocks. At 2s the toggle from the last scene tries to move and springs back, greyed out. At 4s the masked row erases character by character and a fresh one types in. At 7s the toggle finally lands in the on position and the prompt returns a clean exit code.

scenes.narration: Now pick up the laptop. Unsloth shows you the address to type and a code you can scan. The toggle takes effect without a restart, so nothing has to reload.
scenes.on_screen_text: LAN Remote Access: on | address or scannable code

At 3s a laptop glyph slides in from the right and the code reflects onto its screen. At 6s a line draws from laptop to box and lights green. At 9s a RESTART step further along the timeline greys out and a rule strikes through it.

scenes.narration: Here is the part the release notes do not lead with. Server-side tools run as your user. Anyone who reaches that server with your API key can run code on that machine.

At 5s that line detaches and lands at centre on its own. At 8s a second box draws beneath it holding a shell prompt on your machine, with a stranger glyph typing into it.

scenes.narration: That is Unsloth's own banner. It sits on the same docs page as the tunnel. Network reach and code execution are the same switch here. So pass the disable tools flag unless you meant to hand that out.
scenes.visual_brief: The frame splits down the middle. At 2s the left half draws the docs banner with its warning text and the Unsloth mark above it. At 5s the right half types unsloth studio --disable-tools and the shell prompt from the last scene fades to grey. At 8s both halves lock in place and a hairline rule draws between them.

scenes.narration: Now Unsloth answers your laptop from the other room, with nothing in the path. The password change is forced, and the tools decision is yours.
scenes.on_screen_text: LAN access: on | nothing in the path
scenes.visual_brief: The composition returns to frame 1: couch glyph lower left, machine glyph far right. At 2s the wall between them is gone and the request packet slides the whole way across and lands. At 4s the reply types back over the gap in amber. At 6s the wordmark settles into the lower third and the cursor stops blinking.

notes_for_review: One spoken number only, the default bind address, because it is the reason the box ignores the couch. The default port, the 200-plus merged pull requests and the ~190s compaction figure are deliberately unspent: the port is flagged unverified for the desktop app in the brief, and the other two belong to a different feature. No analogy: none of the signature pictures fits a bind address, so the mechanism is stated plain. Two positional labels, not three: the third move is the result and gets the payoff's job.
